title: Articles 9, 10 and 11 beyond protest
subtitle: Belief, expression and association, away from the placard and the police cordon
objectives: Distinguish the forum internum from the forum externum under Article 9, and explain why only manifestation of a belief can lawfully be restricted
Use the four joined claims in Eweida and Others v UK as a worked model of how near-identical facts can produce opposite Article 9 outcomes depending on the strength of the competing justification

Apply Article 10's protection of expression in media, artistic and online contexts, and Article 11's protection of associational autonomy, to fact patterns that are deliberately not protest or assembly cases

leadingAuthorities.citation: Eweida and Others v UK (2013) 57 EHRR 8
leadingAuthorities.role: Four joined claims on religious dress and conduct at work; shows how the same qualified right can succeed or fail on close facts
States that Article 10 protects expression that shocks, offends or disturbs, not only comfortable speech

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Ngole) v University of Sheffield [2019] EWCA Civ 1127
leadingAuthorities.role: Applies Articles 9 and 10 to a social media post and professional fitness-to-practise proceedings
Extends Article 11 to an association's own right to choose its members, outside any assembly context

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students who've done Public law's protest lesson often reach for Ziegler on reflex whenever a fact pattern mentions Articles 10 or 11 — even when nobody in the problem is on a march. This lesson exists to build the other half of the instinct: recognising belief, expression and association claims that never go near a demonstration.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the Article 9/10/11 framework. The test pool here is weighted towards distinguishing similar-looking fact patterns — expect scenarios where the trap is citing the wrong line of authority, not the wrong article.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about the forum internum/forum externum split before moving on — the rest of the lesson assumes you can say, without prompting, which part of Article 9 is absolute and which is qualified.

overview.hook: Public law's lesson on Articles 10 and 11 lives on the street: police cordons, kettling, DPP v Ziegler and the question of when blocking a road is 'lawful excuse'. This lesson deliberately never goes there. Instead: a British Airways check-in desk, a hospital ward, a university social work course, a train drivers' union AGM. Same three articles, same qualified-rights machinery — completely different fact patterns, because most Article 9, 10 and 11 problems a working lawyer meets have nothing to do with a demonstration at all.

parts.heading: Two rights you've already met, from a different angle
parts.voice: signposting — orients students to what this lesson does and does not cover
body: If you've done Public law's lesson on qualified rights and protest, you already know the shape of Articles 10 and 11: a right, a limitation clause, and a proportionality question, usually asked about a march, a cordon or an occupied road. Nothing in that lesson is wrong here — but almost none of it is what this lesson tests. This lesson's facts are a workplace, a newsroom, a comments section, a union membership list. If you find yourself reaching for Ziegler in an answer to one of this lesson's test items, that's the trap this lesson is built to catch.

Article 9 hasn't featured in Public law's spine at all, so start there properly. The Convention right splits into two very differently protected halves. The forum internum is the freedom to hold, or not hold, a religious or other belief — what happens inside your own head. It is absolute: no state interest, however pressing, can justify interfering with it. The forum externum is the freedom to manifest that belief — in worship, teaching, practice and observance — and it is this manifestation limb alone that Article 9(2) allows the state to restrict, on the same 'prescribed by law, legitimate aim, necessary in a democratic society' structure you already know from Article 8.

Articles 10 and 11 keep their familiar qualified-rights structure from Public law — a right in paragraph 1, a limitation clause in paragraph 2 — but this lesson asks what they protect once you take away the demonstration: expression in the press, in art, and online (Article 10); and the freedom to associate with others in clubs, professional bodies and trade unions, not only to assemble with them in a crowd (Article 11).

components.definition: The forum internum is the inward freedom to hold or change a belief, absolutely protected under Article 9(1). The forum externum is the outward manifestation of that belief — worship, teaching, practice, observance — and it alone is subject to the qualifications in Article 9(2).

interaction.prompt: Under Article 9, can the state ever lawfully restrict a person's private, unexpressed religious belief itself (the forum internum), even for a very strong reason?
options: No — the forum internum is absolute; only manifestation can be restricted under Article 9(2)
Yes — if the belief is judged extreme enough, Article 9(2) permits restricting the belief itself
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Article 9(2) only ever reaches manifestation. The moment a problem question is really about restricting what someone believes, rather than what they do or say because of it, you're outside the qualified part of the right altogether.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what Article 9(2) actually qualifies. It lists grounds for restricting manifestation of a belief — worship, teaching, practice, observance — never the belief itself. The forum internum has no limitation clause because it has no visible conduct to limit.

parts.heading: Same right, four claimants, three different outcomes
parts.voice: case-narrative — discovers the doctrine through the facts rather than stating it first
body: Eweida and Others v UK joined four applications from four different British claimants, all alleging their employers had breached Article 9 by restricting religious manifestation at work. Nadia Eweida, a British Airways check-in employee, was told to remove a small silver cross worn visibly over her uniform, under a policy restricting jewellery; she was moved to unpaid duties and eventually disciplined for continuing to wear it. Shirley Chaplin, a geriatric ward nurse, was told to remove a similar cross on a chain for uniform reasons and, when she refused, was moved to a non-nursing role. Lillian Ladele, a local authority registrar, refused on religious grounds to conduct civil partnership ceremonies and faced disciplinary proceedings for failing to comply with the council's dignity-at-work and non-discrimination policy. Gary McFarlane, a relationship counsellor at Relate, was dismissed after saying he might have conscientious objections to providing psycho-sexual therapy to same-sex couples.

All four claimants said the same thing: a genuine manifestation of religious belief, restricted by an employer. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 9 for exactly one of them — Eweida. For Chaplin, Ladele and McFarlane, it found no violation at all. Learning Eweida as 'the case that protects religious dress at work' badly misreads what the judgment actually does: three of its four claimants lost.

The difference was never about the sincerity of anyone's belief — the Court accepted all four as genuine. It was about the weight of the competing justification on each set of facts. BA's uniform policy served only a corporate image interest, was inconsistently enforced against other staff, and a small discreet cross posed no plausible risk to anyone; the domestic courts had given that interest disproportionate weight against Eweida's right. Chaplin's hospital, by contrast, could point to a specific, evidenced safety risk — a chain or cross could be grabbed by a confused or combative patient, or interfere with clinical procedures — which the Court accepted as a materially stronger justification. Ladele's and McFarlane's employers were enforcing a non-discrimination policy protecting service users (same-sex couples) from being refused a service on grounds of their sexual orientation; the Court held states have a wide margin of appreciation to prioritise that protection over an employee's religious objection to providing the service. Read together, the four claims are a masterclass in how fact-sensitive Article 9(2) proportionality really is: the article did the same work every time, and the facts did all the deciding.

components.factsShort: Four UK employees — a BA check-in worker, an NHS nurse, a registrar and a relationship counsellor — separately claimed their employers' restrictions on manifesting their Christian beliefs at work breached Article 9.
components.ratioShort: Article 9(2) manifestation claims turn on the proportionality of the specific justification advanced on the facts, not on any general rule about religious dress or conduct at work; near-identical-looking claims can be decided oppositely.

expanded.facts: Eweida and Chaplin both wanted to wear a visible cross with their uniform and were restricted by employer dress codes; Ladele and McFarlane both wanted to be excused, on religious grounds, from parts of their job duties relating to service users' sexual orientation, and were disciplined or dismissed for refusing to perform those duties.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that a fair balance had not been struck in Eweida's case: the domestic courts had placed too much weight on BA's wish to project a certain corporate image, against too little weight on Eweida's fundamental right, where there was no evidence the small and discreet cross had any real impact on that image and where BA had in fact accommodated other forms of religious dress. In Chaplin's case, by contrast, the hospital's justification — patient and staff safety on a ward, including the risk of a chain being pulled during contact with confused or dementia patients — was found to be substantially more weighty, and the interference proportionate. In Ladele's and McFarlane's cases, the Court held that states enjoy a wide margin of appreciation in reconciling employees' religious beliefs with an employer's policy of providing services without discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that the employers were entitled to give priority to that non-discrimination aim.
expanded.significance: Eweida is the leading illustration that Article 9(2) proportionality is not a doctrine you can answer by naming the right case — it has to be argued on the specific weight of the interference against the specific weight of the justification, every time. It also shows that a state's margin of appreciation can widen sharply where the interference protects a third party's own Convention-adjacent interest, such as a service user's protection from discrimination.

interaction.prompt: Two employees, both disciplined for wearing a visible religious symbol at work. Which scenario more closely mirrors Eweida's successful claim, rather than Chaplin's unsuccessful one?
interaction.scenarioA: An office receptionist is told to remove a small pendant worn on a thin chain, under a general 'no visible jewellery' policy applied inconsistently — colleagues wear visible piercings and wedding rings without comment — and there is no evidence the pendant poses any safety or operational risk.
interaction.scenarioB: An operating theatre nurse is told to remove a pendant on a chain under an infection-control and patient-handling policy, after clinical staff identify a specific risk that it could be grabbed by a disoriented patient or catch on equipment during a procedure.
interaction.explanation: A tracks Eweida: a weak, inconsistently applied justification against a discreet manifestation, which the Court found disproportionate. B tracks Chaplin: a specific, evidenced safety justification, which the Court found weighty enough to justify the restriction. The symbol and the discipline look identical in both — only the strength of the competing justification differs, which is exactly the point Eweida is teaching.

parts.heading: Article 10 without a placard: Handyside, and expression that offends
parts.voice: argumentative — states the counter-intuitive principle before testing it
body: Article 10's most quoted line comes from a case about neither protest nor politics but an obscenity prosecution over a schoolbook. In Handyside v UK, a publisher was convicted for publishing The Little Red Schoolbook, which included frank material on sex aimed at children and teenagers. The European Court of Human Rights upheld the conviction on the facts — but in doing so stated a principle that reaches far beyond the case: freedom of expression under Article 10 applies 'not only to information or ideas that are favourably received... but also to those that offend, shock or disturb the State or any sector of the population,' because pluralism, tolerance and broadmindedness are what a democratic society actually requires.

That principle is what turns Article 10 into a genuinely uncomfortable right to apply, because it means the article's hardest cases are never about speech everyone already agrees is fine. Media reporting that embarrasses a public figure, artistic work that offends religious sensibilities, and — increasingly — opinions posted online that a professional body or employer finds unacceptable, all sit inside Article 10's protection in principle; the qualified-rights machinery then asks whether restricting them is a proportionate response to a legitimate aim, exactly as it would for any other Article 10 claim.

R (Ngole) v University of Sheffield shows this machinery applied to a fact pattern many students initially misclassify as 'just a professional conduct case.' Felix Ngole, a postgraduate social work student, posted comments on a public news article's Facebook comment thread, in his personal capacity, expressing a Christian view — citing scripture — that he did not endorse same-sex marriage. The posts were not directed at any individual, and did not incite hatred or refuse to work with anyone. The university's fitness-to-practise panel removed him from the course, reasoning that the views expressed were incompatible with the professional standards expected of a social worker. The Court of Appeal held the university's decision had not properly weighed Ngole's Article 9 and Article 10 rights against the regulatory concern, and was disproportionate: expressing a mainstream religious viewpoint on a matter of public debate, in general and temperate terms not directed at a specific service user, is not automatically incompatible with fitness to practise, even where a regulator or institution finds the viewpoint objectionable.

components.factsShort: A social work student posted Facebook comments, in a personal capacity, expressing a religious objection to same-sex marriage; the university removed him from the course on fitness-to-practise grounds.
components.ratioShort: A regulator or institution must properly balance Articles 9 and 10 against its professional standards concern; removal was disproportionate where the views were general, temperate and not directed at any service user.

expanded.facts: Ngole commented on a public news article about a US county clerk who had refused to issue same-sex marriage licences, citing biblical passages to explain his own view that homosexual conduct was sinful. He did not name any individual, did not suggest he would refuse to work with LGBT service users, and made the comments outside any professional context.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that the fitness-to-practise panel had failed to engage properly with the balancing exercise required by Articles 9 and 10: it had treated the expression of a traditional religious viewpoint as inherently and automatically incompatible with the professional role, without asking whether, on these specific facts — general, non-targeted, off-duty comments on a matter of public debate — removal from the course was a proportionate response.
expanded.significance: Ngole is the leading modern illustration that professional regulation cannot simply assume that holding or expressing a mainstream religious or moral view is incompatible with fitness to practise; the regulator must still do the Article 9/10 proportionality exercise on the actual facts, including whether the expression was targeted at, or likely to affect trust and confidence with, service users.

interaction.prompt: Which of the following best captures what Handyside actually establishes about Article 10?
options: Article 10 only protects speech that is inoffensive and widely accepted, since anything shocking falls outside the right entirely

Article 10's protection extends in principle to expression that offends, shocks or disturbs — the qualified-rights structure then asks whether restricting it is proportionate, not whether it was protected at all
Article 10 gives an absolute right to publish any material, however offensive, without restriction
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer treats offensive speech as automatically unprotected — but Handyside says the opposite: it is squarely within Article 10(1)'s scope. What the case actually did was uphold a restriction on it as proportionate under Article 10(2), on those specific facts. Confusing 'protected in principle' with 'never restrictable' is the most common misreading of this case.

parts.heading: Article 11 without a march: an association's right to choose its own members
parts.voice: structural — builds the doctrine as a reference point before applying it
body: Public law's protest lesson treats Article 11 almost entirely as freedom of assembly — the right to gather with others in a particular place, at a particular time, usually to demonstrate. That is one half of the article. The other half, freedom of association, protects something structurally different: the ongoing relationship between a person and an organisation — a trade union, a political party, a professional body, a club — and it protects both the individual's right to join or leave, and, less intuitively, the organisation's own right to decide who it will and will not have as a member.

ASLEF v UK is the clearest illustration of that second, organisation-facing dimension. The train drivers' union ASLEF expelled a member, Mr Lee, who was an active member and election candidate for the British National Party, a far-right political party whose aims the union considered fundamentally opposed to its own values of anti-racism and anti-fascism. Under UK law at the time, statutory protection against exclusion or expulsion from a trade union meant Lee could not lawfully be expelled purely for his political party membership, and he successfully brought a domestic claim against the union for unlawful expulsion.

The union then took the case to Strasbourg — arguing that being forced to retain a member whose political activities were fundamentally at odds with its own democratic and ideological character breached the union's own Article 11 rights. The European Court of Human Rights agreed: freedom of association protects an association's autonomy to determine its own membership according to its own ideological commitments, and a state's near-blanket statutory protection against expulsion, applied without regard to that autonomy, was itself a violation of Article 11. It is a genuinely useful case to hold onto, because it flips the usual framing — here it is the collective body, not an individual protester, whose Article 11 right is in play.

components.factsShort: A trade union expelled a member for active membership of a political party whose aims it considered incompatible with its own; UK law prevented the expulsion, and the union claimed this breached its own Article 11 rights.
components.ratioShort: Freedom of association under Article 11 protects an association's own autonomy to decide, on ideological grounds, who may belong to it — a state cannot impose near-absolute protection against expulsion without regard to that associational autonomy.

expanded.facts: Mr Lee was a long-standing ASLEF member who stood as a BNP candidate. ASLEF's rules allowed expulsion of members belonging to political parties whose policies conflicted with the union's own objectives; Lee was expelled on that basis, but succeeded in a domestic claim that the expulsion was unlawful under employment legislation protecting union membership.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that Article 11 does not only protect an individual against exclusion from an association — it also protects the association's freedom to choose its members and to organise itself in accordance with its own values. A trade union with clearly stated anti-racist and anti-fascist objectives could not be compelled to retain a member whose political activities were fundamentally incompatible with those objectives; the domestic law's inflexible protection went further than Article 11 permitted.
expanded.significance: ASLEF is the standard authority for associational autonomy as a distinct strand of Article 11, separate from freedom of assembly, and for the idea that Article 11 claims can run in favour of the organisation itself, not only its individual members or those excluded from it.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below adapted from ASLEF v UK, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
interaction.passage: The applicant union had expelled a member because his continued political activities were incompatible with the union's stated aims. Article 11 protects not only the right of individuals to join associations but also the right of associations to determine, in accordance with their own ideological objectives, who may be a member of them. A state which affords members near-absolute statutory protection against expulsion, without allowing an association any means of enforcing its own basic values, restricts the association's freedom of association disproportionately.
interaction.ratioSentence: Article 11 protects not only the right of individuals to join associations but also the right of associations to determine, in accordance with their own ideological objectives, who may be a member of them.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sentence doing the doctrinal work. Everything before it is the fact pattern; everything after it is the application of that principle to this particular statutory scheme.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence that states a general proposition about what Article 11 protects, rather than describing these specific facts or this specific statute. The ratio is the principle the rest of the reasoning is applying.

parts.heading: Building the answer: don't reach for Ziegler by reflex
parts.voice: direct — practical exam guidance, closes by naming the trap explicitly
body: The most useful skill this lesson can leave you with isn't a longer list of case names — it's a habit of checking, before you write a word of analysis, whether a fact pattern is actually a protest/assembly case at all. If nobody in the problem is occupying a space, marching, demonstrating or being arrested for obstruction, DPP v Ziegler and the 'lawful excuse' proportionality framework from Public law's lesson are very unlikely to be the right authorities — even if the problem mentions Articles 10 or 11 by name.

The workplace, media, online-expression and associational-autonomy fact patterns in this lesson call for a different toolkit: identify which article and which limb is engaged (forum externum manifestation under Article 9; expression under Article 10; association, not assembly, under Article 11); identify the specific interference and who imposed it; then run the standard qualified-rights structure — prescribed by law, legitimate aim, necessary in a democratic society, proportionate — using the weight of the actual competing justification on these facts, the way Eweida's four claimants show you have to.

Treat the six authorities in this lesson as a toolkit for that structure, not a menu to cite by pattern-matching on surface facts: Eweida for how proportionality can point opposite ways on similar-looking manifestation claims; Handyside for the scope of protected expression, however unwelcome; Ngole for how professional regulation must still do the balancing exercise rather than assume incompatibility; and ASLEF for the associational, non-assembly, dimension of Article 11.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students frequently cite DPP v Ziegler or the 'lawful excuse' proportionality framework from protest cases when analysing a workplace religious dress dispute, an online expression case, or a trade union membership dispute, simply because the problem mentions Article 10 or Article 11.
components.whyItsWrong: Ziegler's framework is built around a specific statutory offence (obstruction) and the particular proportionality questions that arise when the state restricts assembly in a public place. None of that machinery fits a workplace, media or associational-autonomy fact pattern. Citing it signals that you've spotted the article but not the actual legal question — examiners read this as pattern-matching, not analysis.

interaction.prompt: Amara, a trainee paramedic, posts on her personal, non-work social media account — in a thread about a news story on assisted dying — a comment stating her Christian view that assisted dying is morally wrong, without addressing any patient or colleague. Her ambulance trust's fitness-to-practise panel removes her from the training programme, reasoning that her posts are incompatible with 'patient-centred, non-judgmental' professional values. Analyse whether the removal is compatible with her Convention rights.
factsToOrder: Amara posts in a personal capacity, outside any work context
The comment expresses a general religious viewpoint on a public debate
The comment is not directed at, or about, any identifiable patient or colleague
The trust removes her from training, citing incompatibility with professional values
No evidence is given that the comment affected her actual clinical practice or patient trust

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether removing Amara from her training programme for expressing a personal religious view online is a proportionate interference with her rights under Articles 9 and 10.
modelAnswer.rule: Manifestation of belief and expression are qualified rights: an interference must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be necessary in a democratic society (proportionate). Following Ngole, a professional body may not treat expression of a mainstream religious or moral viewpoint as automatically incompatible with fitness to practise; it must weigh the actual impact of the specific expression — whether it was targeted at, or likely to undermine trust with, service users — against the regulatory concern. Following Handyside, the fact that a view is unwelcome or contested is not itself a reason to restrict it.
modelAnswer.application: Amara's comment was made off-duty, in a personal capacity, expressed a viewpoint on a genuine matter of public debate, and — critically, as in Ngole — was not directed at, or about, any identifiable patient or colleague. There is no evidence her clinical practice or patient trust was actually affected. On these facts the trust's justification looks closer to Ngole's disproportionate removal than to a case with real, evidenced harm to patient care.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The removal is likely to be a disproportionate interference with Amara's Article 9 and Article 10 rights, following Ngole, unless the trust can point to some specific evidenced risk to patient trust or care that this problem does not disclose.

testPool.prompt: Name the two components Article 9 is split into, and state which one is absolute.
acceptableAnswers: forum internum and forum externum, forum internum is absolute
testPool.modelAnswer: Article 9 splits into the forum internum (the freedom to hold a belief, which is absolute) and the forum externum (the freedom to manifest that belief, which is qualified under Article 9(2)).

testPool.prompt: In Eweida and Others v UK, how many of the four joined claimants succeeded in establishing an Article 9 violation?
options: One
All four

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT a ground listed in Article 9(2) on which manifestation of a belief may be restricted?
options: Public safety
Protection of public order, health or morals
Protection of the rights and freedoms of others
Preservation of a particular religion's dominant social status
testPool.trapExplanation: Article 9(2)'s grounds are public safety, protection of public order/health/morals, and protection of the rights and freedoms of others — all aimed at competing interests, never at privileging one belief system over another. Preserving a religion's social dominance is not a Convention-recognised legitimate aim at all.

testPool.prompt: Under Handyside v UK, does Article 10 protect expression that offends or shocks a section of the population?
options: Yes — in principle, subject to the Article 10(2) qualification analysis
No — offensive expression falls outside Article 10 entirely

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors Ladele's unsuccessful claim in Eweida and Others v UK?
testPool.scenarioA: A council registrar refuses, on religious grounds, to conduct civil partnership ceremonies, and is disciplined for failing to comply with the council's non-discrimination policy towards service users.
testPool.scenarioB: A council office worker wears a small religious pendant under a general no-jewellery policy that is otherwise unenforced against colleagues wearing visible jewellery.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors Ladele: an employee's religious objection is weighed against an employer's non-discrimination duty towards service users, and the ECtHR gave states a wide margin of appreciation to prioritise that duty. B is closer to Eweida's facts — a weak, inconsistently enforced justification against a discreet manifestation.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most supports treating the university's decision as disproportionate, applying Ngole.
testPool.scenarioText: A trainee teacher posts, on a personal account, a general comment referencing his faith's traditional teaching on marriage, in response to a public news article. He does not name or address any pupil, colleague or parent. His training provider removes him from the course, citing incompatibility with professional values.
tappableSpans: referencing his faith's traditional teaching on marriage
does not name or address any pupil, colleague or parent
testPool.correctSpan: does not name or address any pupil, colleague or parent
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the fact Ngole turns on: expression aimed at nobody in particular, on a matter of public debate, is much harder to justify restricting than expression targeted at, or affecting trust with, an actual service user.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on who, if anyone, the comment is directed at. Ngole's reasoning distinguishes general, untargeted expression of a viewpoint from expression aimed at or about an identifiable service user — the latter is far easier for a regulator to justify restricting.

testPool.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court applies them when assessing an Article 9(2) or Article 10(2) restriction.
items: Confirm the right is engaged (manifestation or expression, not merely private belief)
Ask whether the interference is prescribed by law
Ask whether the interference pursues a legitimate aim listed in the qualification clause
Ask whether the interference is necessary in a democratic society and proportionate to that aim

testPool.prompt: Article 11(1) protects freedom of peaceful assembly 'and freedom of association with others, including the right to form and to join trade unions for the protection of his interests.' Based on ASLEF v UK, which reading of 'freedom of association' is correct?
options: It only protects an individual's right to join an association; associations themselves have no Article 11 rights
It protects both an individual's right to join or leave an association and the association's own autonomy to decide who may belong to it
It applies only to trade unions, not to political parties, clubs or professional bodies
testPool.explanation: ASLEF confirms that freedom of association is a two-way protection: it covers the individual member and the collective body's own ideological autonomy over its membership.

testPool.prompt: A political party's local branch expels a member after he begins publicly campaigning for a rival party's platform while still claiming membership. The member argues this breaches his Article 11 rights. On ASLEF's reasoning, is the expulsion likely to be a breach?
options: No — a political association's own Article 11 autonomy allows it to expel a member whose activities are fundamentally at odds with its own aims
Yes — Article 11 gives every member an unqualified right to remain a member regardless of their conduct
Yes — but only because political parties, unlike trade unions, have no associational autonomy at all
testPool.explanation: ASLEF's reasoning is not limited to trade unions; it rests on the general principle that associations may determine, according to their own values, who belongs to them. A member actively campaigning for a rival platform is analogous to Lee's incompatible political activity.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Handyside v UK, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The Court has consistently held that freedom of expression constitutes one of the essential foundations of a democratic society. Subject to Article 10(2), it is applicable not only to 'information' or 'ideas' that are favourably received or regarded as inoffensive, but also to those that offend, shock or disturb the State or any sector of the population. Such are the demands of pluralism, tolerance and broadmindedness without which there is no 'democratic society'. On the facts, the domestic courts' assessment that the publication required restriction fell within the national margin of appreciation.
testPool.ratioSentence: Subject to Article 10(2), it is applicable not only to 'information' or 'ideas' that are favourably received or regarded as inoffensive, but also to those that offend, shock or disturb the State or any sector of the population.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Article 10 protects artistic or online expression only when it is politically significant, rather than merely personal or creative?
sliderLabels: Only politically significant expression is protected
Personal, creative and everyday expression is protected too
testPool.correctPosition: Personal, creative and everyday expression is protected too
testPool.explanation: Article 10's scope is broad: it protects the receipt and imparting of 'information and ideas' generally, not only political speech. Handyside itself concerned a book, not a political statement, and later case law extends the same reasoning to art and online expression.

testPool.prompt: A magazine publishes a satirical cartoon mocking a religious leader's public statements on a political issue. The religious leader's followers complain, and a regulator fines the magazine for content 'likely to cause serious offence'. Analyse whether the fine is compatible with Article 10.
factsToOrder: The cartoon comments on a public figure's political statements
The content is satirical rather than a factual claim
Followers of the religious leader find the content seriously offensive
A regulator imposes a fine specifically for causing offence
No claim is made that the cartoon incites violence or hatred

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether fining the magazine purely for causing serious offence is a proportionate restriction on its Article 10 rights.
modelAnswer.rule: Following Handyside, Article 10 protects expression that offends, shocks or disturbs; a restriction must still be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be necessary and proportionate — offensiveness alone is not, without more, a sufficient justification, particularly for satire commenting on a public figure's public statements.
modelAnswer.application: The cartoon addresses a public figure's political statements — core Article 10 territory — using satire, a recognised and protected mode of expression. That it causes serious offence to followers is, on Handyside's own terms, not a reason to remove it from protection; there is no suggestion of incitement to violence or hatred, which would raise a materially different and stronger justification.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A fine based purely on causing serious offence, without more, is likely to be a disproportionate interference with Article 10, since offensiveness on its own does not defeat the right Handyside describes.

testPool.prompt: A professional body's disciplinary code bars any social media post that 'might embarrass the profession'. Using it, the body sanctions a member for a private, off-duty, non-targeted comment on a religious topic. Which is the strongest ground of challenge?
options: That the code itself is void, since professional bodies can never regulate members' off-duty conduct

That the sanction is likely disproportionate under Articles 9/10, applying Ngole, because it treats a general, non-targeted religious viewpoint as automatically incompatible with the profession without weighing the actual facts
That the member has an absolute Article 9 right to say anything, since belief is absolute
testPool.trapExplanation: The first option overstates the case — professional bodies can regulate off-duty conduct in principle, provided restrictions are proportionate. The third confuses the absolute forum internum with the always-qualified forum externum. Ngole's actual contribution is the middle ground: the regulator must do the balancing exercise properly, on the specific facts, rather than assume incompatibility.
